lessons.title: Lesson 1: CDL classes and endorsements: which one do you need?
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Match a driving job to the CDL class and endorsements it needs.
This lesson builds toward: Given a description of a driving job, you will identify the CDL class (A, B or C) and any endorsements the job needs, getting at least 4 of 5 job descriptions right.
A commercial driver's license (CDL) lets you drive large or special vehicles for work. There are three classes, based on the vehicle.
Class A is for combination vehicles, like a tractor pulling a trailer, when the combination is rated at 26,001 pounds or more and the towed trailer is rated over 10,000 pounds. Class B is for one big vehicle rated at 26,001 pounds or more, like a dump truck, box truck or city bus; it may tow a small trailer rated 10,000 pounds or less. Class C is for smaller vehicles that carry 16 or more people (counting the driver) or carry hazardous materials that need placards.
Endorsements are extra letters on your license for special work. T: double or triple trailers. P: passengers. N: tank vehicles. H: hazardous materials. X: tank plus hazardous materials. S: school bus. Each needs its own test, and the H endorsement also needs a security background check.
Start from the job you want. Read real job ads near you and look for the class and endorsements they ask for.
Step by step:
- Pick a job you want, such as long-haul, local delivery, bus or dump truck.
- Ask: does it pull a big trailer? That is usually Class A.
- Is it one big truck or bus? That is usually Class B.
- Does it carry passengers, liquids in a tank, double trailers or hazardous materials? Add the endorsement.
Words to know:
- CDL: commercial driver's license: the license needed to drive large or special vehicles for work.
- Combination vehicle: a truck that pulls a trailer, like a tractor-trailer.
- Weight rating: the most a vehicle is built to weigh fully loaded, set by the maker (often called GVWR).
- Endorsement: an extra permission on your CDL for special work, such as passengers or tanks.
- Hazardous materials (hazmat): goods that can hurt people or property, like fuel or chemicals, that need warning signs called placards.
Official sources:
- 49 CFR 383.91: Commercial motor vehicle groups (Cornell LII copy of the federal rule)
- 49 CFR 383.153: Endorsement codes on the CDL and CLP
- FMCSA: Commercial Driver's License (the official federal CDL pages)
Try it now: Find three real driving job ads near you (on a job site or a company's own site). For each, write the job, the CDL class it asks for and any endorsements. Circle the job you want most.
You can now match a driving job to Class A, B or C and name the endorsements it needs.

check.q: A job is driving a tractor pulling a 53-foot trailer. Which class is it usually?
check.why: A tractor pulling a heavy trailer is a combination vehicle, which is Class A.

check.q: Which endorsement do you add to drive a school bus?
check.why: S is the school bus endorsement; the P passenger endorsement is also needed for buses.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The steps from permit to license
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the steps to a CDL in order and who handles each one.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official FMCSA and state sources, you will list the steps from medical exam to CDL skills test in the right order, with no step missing and the waiting time and training rule included.
Most new drivers follow the same steps. The federal rules come from FMCSA; your state's driver licensing office runs the tests and sets the fees and forms.
First, a medical exam (often called a DOT physical) from a certified medical examiner. Most drivers must pass it again at least every 24 months. Second, pass the state's written knowledge tests to get a commercial learner's permit (CLP). Federal rules say a CLP holder must be at least 18 and must wait at least 14 days before the skills test. While you practice on public roads, a CDL holder with the right class must sit next to you.
Since February 7, 2022, most people getting a first Class A or B CDL, or a first P, S or H endorsement, must finish entry-level driver training (ELDT) with a provider listed on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry before the test. Then you take the state skills test: pre-trip inspection, basic vehicle control and on-road driving.
Age: to drive across state lines you must be at least 21. Some states allow drivers aged 18 to 20 inside the state only. Check your state's rules.
Step by step:
- Medical exam with a certified medical examiner.
- Study the state CDL manual and pass the knowledge tests.
- Get your commercial learner's permit (CLP).
- Finish entry-level driver training with a registered provider, if it applies to you.
- Practice with a qualified CDL holder beside you; wait at least 14 days.
- Take the skills test: pre-trip inspection, basic control, on-road driving.
Words to know:
- FMCSA: the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, the U.S. agency that sets the rules for trucks and buses.
- CLP: commercial learner's permit: lets you practice driving a commercial vehicle with a qualified CDL holder beside you.
- ELDT: entry-level driver training: the federal training most new CDL drivers must finish before testing.
- Training Provider Registry: FMCSA's official list of schools and employers allowed to give ELDT.
- Medical examiner: a health professional certified to do the DOT physical for commercial drivers.
Official sources:
- 49 CFR 383.25: Commercial learner's permit (CLP)
- 49 CFR 380.603: Who must complete entry-level driver training
- FMCSA Training Provider Registry (ELDT)
- 49 CFR 391.11: Driver qualifications (age, English, medical)
- 49 CFR 391.45: When drivers must be medically examined
- 49 CFR 383.113: What the CDL skills test covers
Try it now: Look up your state's CDL page (search your state name plus "CDL" and open the .gov site). Write the six steps in order and, next to each, what your state says about it: the forms, where to go and the fees it lists.
You can now list the steps from medical exam to skills test in order and say who handles each one.

check.q: You just got your CLP. How soon can you take the skills test under federal rules?
check.why: Federal rules say a CLP holder must wait at least 14 days before taking the skills test.

check.q: Where do you find a school that can give the required entry-level driver training?
check.why: Only providers on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry can give the required training.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Studying for the knowledge tests
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a study routine with your state's CDL manual and score a practice set.
This lesson builds toward: Using your state's free CDL manual, you will set up a study routine for the knowledge tests you need and score a practice set, reaching at least 8 of 10 on practice questions before you book the test.
Every state has a free CDL manual on its driver licensing website. The written tests come from it, so it is the best study book you can have.
Most new drivers take General Knowledge. Many also take Air Brakes (most big trucks use air brakes) and Combination Vehicles (for Class A). Each endorsement has its own test. Your state manual lists which sections go with which test.
Study one section at a time. Read it, close the manual, and write three things you learned. Then use the practice questions in the manual or on your state's site. Aim for at least 8 of 10 right before you book the real test.
Be careful with paid apps and websites that promise the "real test questions". Free practice from your state is enough for most people.
Step by step:
- Download your state's CDL manual from the official .gov site.
- Mark the sections you need: General Knowledge plus the ones for your class and endorsements.
- Plan one section per study session, 20 to 30 minutes.
- After each section, write three things you learned without looking.
- Do practice questions until you get at least 8 of 10 right.
Words to know:
- Knowledge test: the written (often computer) test you pass to get your CLP.
- Air brakes: brakes worked by compressed air, used on most heavy trucks and buses.
- CDL manual: your state's official study book for the CDL tests.
Official sources:
- FMCSA: Commercial Driver's License (the official federal CDL pages)
Try it now: Download your state's CDL manual. Read the first part of the General Knowledge section about vehicle inspection. Close it and write three things you remember. Then write five practice questions of your own with answers, and swap with a study partner or check them against the manual.
You can now find your state's CDL manual, pick the sections you need, and study them in short sessions until you score 8 of 10.

check.q: What is the best free study book for your CDL knowledge tests?
options: A paid app with "real test answers"
A video from a stranger online
check.why: The written tests come from your state's official CDL manual.

check.q: You want a Class A for tractor-trailers with air brakes. Which tests do you usually need?
options: General Knowledge, Air Brakes and Combination Vehicles
check.why: Most Class A tractor-trailer drivers take General Knowledge, Air Brakes and Combination Vehicles.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The pre-trip inspection
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Name each area of a pre-trip inspection and what you check there.
This lesson builds toward: Standing at a truck or using a picture of one, you will name each part you check in a pre-trip inspection and say what you check on it, covering all the main areas in order with no area skipped.
The skills test starts with a pre-trip inspection. You walk around the vehicle, point to each part, and say out loud what you are checking. Federal rules also say every driver must make sure the vehicle is safe before driving it, so this is a habit for your whole career.
Go in the same order every time, so you never skip a part. A common order is: engine compartment, cab and engine start, steering, suspension, brakes, wheels and tires, the sides and rear with lights, and the coupling area on a combination vehicle. On air-brake vehicles you also check the air brake gauges and warnings.
For each part, say what makes it safe: "Mounted securely, not cracked or bent, no leaks." Your state manual has the full list for your vehicle type. Your training provider will show you on a real truck.
If you find a defect, the truck does not move until it is fixed. Report it and write it down.
Step by step:
- Use the checklist from your state manual for your vehicle type.
- Start at the engine compartment, then the cab, then walk around the truck in the same order every time.
- Point to each part and say what you check: mounted, not damaged, no leaks.
- Check lights, reflectors and tires on every side.
- Write down and report any defect; do not drive until it is fixed.
Words to know:
- Pre-trip inspection: the safety check a driver does on a vehicle before driving it.
- Defect: a broken, worn or missing part that makes a vehicle unsafe.
- Coupling: the parts that connect a tractor to a trailer, like the fifth wheel and kingpin.
- Fifth wheel: the flat, round plate on a tractor that the trailer locks onto.
Official sources:
- 49 CFR 383.113: What the CDL skills test covers
- 49 CFR 396.13: Driver inspection before driving
Try it now: Using the inspection section of your state CDL manual, write a pre-trip checklist for the vehicle you plan to test in. Then practice saying it out loud on a car, a picture of a truck, or a toy truck: point to each area and say what you check.
You can now walk through a pre-trip inspection in order and say what you check on each part.

check.q: Why do you inspect in the same order every time?
options: So you never skip a part
Because it is faster to skip parts
Because the examiner chooses the order
check.why: A fixed order means no area gets missed.

check.q: During your pre-trip you find a cracked brake hose. What do you do?
options: Drive slowly to the next stop
Report it, write it down and do not drive until it is fixed
Ignore it if the brakes still work
check.why: A safety defect means the vehicle does not move until it is repaired.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Basic control and safe driving habits
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the safe action in common truck driving situations.
This lesson builds toward: Given a driving situation, you will choose the safe action for space, speed, backing and driver fitness, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right.
After the pre-trip, the skills test checks basic vehicle control (moving forward and backward, backing in a straight line and around a curve, and turning) and on-road driving.
Examiners look for safe habits. Keep a big space cushion: trucks need much more room to stop than cars. Slow down for rain, snow, curves, work zones and heavy traffic, even below the speed limit. Scan far ahead and check your mirrors often. Make wide right turns carefully so the trailer does not hit the curb or a car.
Back up as little as possible. If you are not sure what is behind you, get out and look. Many drivers remember G.O.A.L.: Get Out And Look.
You must also be fit to drive. Federal hours of service rules limit how long you can drive and work before you rest, and drivers are tested for drugs and alcohol. Never drive tired, ill or impaired.
Step by step:
- Keep a large gap in front; add more in bad weather.
- Set your speed for the road, weather and load, not just the sign.
- Check your mirrors every few seconds and before every lane change.
- Before backing: Get Out And Look, then back slowly.
- Stop and rest when you are tired; follow hours of service rules.
Words to know:
- Space cushion: the empty space you keep around your vehicle so you have room to stop or steer.
- Off-tracking: when the rear wheels of a long vehicle follow a shorter path than the front wheels in a turn.
- Hours of service: FMCSA rules on how long a driver may drive and work before resting.
Official sources:
- 49 CFR 383.113: What the CDL skills test covers
- FMCSA: Hours of service rules
Try it now: Write down five situations from your state manual's safe driving section (for example rain at night, a work zone, backing into a dock). For each, write the safe action in one sentence. Ask a study partner to quiz you on them.
You can now choose the safe action for space, speed, backing and fitness to drive.

check.q: You are backing into a loading dock and cannot see a corner. What do you do?
options: Get out and look before you keep backing
check.why: G.O.A.L.: Get Out And Look when you are not sure what is behind you.

check.q: It starts to rain hard on the highway. What is the safe choice?
options: Keep the same speed and gap
Follow the car ahead more closely to see its lights
Speed up to get out of the rain
Slow down and increase your following distance
check.why: Wet roads mean longer stopping distances, so slow down and leave more space.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Choosing training and making your CDL plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a dated CDL plan with registered training providers you can contact.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official FMCSA and state sources, you will list the steps from medical exam to CDL skills test in the right order, with no step missing and the waiting time and training rule included. Using your state's free CDL manual, you will set up a study routine for the knowledge tests you need and score a practice set, reaching at least 8 of 10 on practice questions before you book the test.
Before you pay for or sign up for any training, check that the school or employer is listed on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry. You can search the registry by location.
Some trucking companies pay for training if you agree to drive for them for a set time. Read the contract carefully: what happens if you leave early? Will you have to pay the training back? Ask before you sign.
Veterans: if you drove heavy military vehicles, ask your state about a military skills test waiver; FMCSA allows states to offer one to qualifying service members and recent veterans. If you have a record, call the state licensing office and ask employers about their hiring rules early; a hazmat endorsement also needs a security check.
Now turn it into a plan. A plan with dates is much more likely to happen than a wish.
Step by step:
- Write the job you want and the class and endorsements it needs.
- Search the Training Provider Registry and list three providers near you.
- Call or visit; ask about the schedule, the total cost, the contract and job placement.
- Put a target date next to every step, from the medical exam to the skills test.
- Plan which manual sections you will study each week.
Words to know:
- Training contract: an agreement that a company pays for your training if you work for it for a set time.
- Skills test waiver: a choice some states offer to skip the CDL skills test for qualifying military drivers.
Official sources:
- FMCSA Training Provider Registry (ELDT)
- 49 CFR 383.77: Skills test waiver for military drivers
- 49 CFR 380.603: Who must complete entry-level driver training
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers
Try it now: Search the Training Provider Registry for three providers near you. Write their names, how to contact them, and three questions you will ask each one. Then put a target date next to each step of your CDL path.
You can now check that a training provider is registered and write a CDL plan with a date for every step.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Right license The class or endorsements do not match the job, or are missing. The class and every endorsement match the target job and a real job ad. Also notes a second job the same license would open, or an endorsement to add later. Steps in order Steps are missing or out of order, or the training rule or 14-day wait is left out. All steps are in order with a target date each, including the medical exam, CLP, training and 14-day wait. Each step also names the office or website that handles it. Registered training No providers, or providers not checked on the registry. Three providers from the Training Provider Registry with contact details. Includes the answers to questions asked: cost, schedule, contract terms. Study plan No study plan, or it does not use the state manual. Weekly sections of the state manual for every test needed, with a practice score goal. Includes practice scores already reached. Pre-trip checklist The checklist skips main areas or is not in a fixed order. Covers every main area in a fixed order, with what to check on each part. The learner can say it out loud, pointing to the parts, without reading. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check your plan again.

check.q: A school says it gives CDL training but is not on the Training Provider Registry. What should you do?
options: Sign up fast before the price goes up
Pay cash so it is cheaper
Choose a provider that is on the registry
Ask a friend to check it for you later
check.why: Training that counts for most new drivers must come from a provider on FMCSA's registry.

check.q: Which plan is most likely to work?
options: "Medical exam by May 3, knowledge tests by May 24, study one manual section each week."
"I'll take the test and see what happens."
check.why: A plan with dates and weekly study steps turns a goal into actions.
